title: Using JA4+ Fingerprints for Device Identification in Encrypted IoT Networks
content: This paper investigates whether JA4+ fingerprint decomposition improves passive identification of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in encrypted network environments, without incorporating payload inspection or active probing techniques. As TLS encryption and privacy-preserving mechanisms such as Encrypted Client Hello reduce the visibility of application-layer metadata, traditional payload- and domain-based identification techniques become less effective. JA4+ fingerprints provide an alternative approach by extracting observable characteristics from TLS handshakes, certificates, and transport-layer metadata without requiring traffic decryption. The proposed methodology evaluates different JA4+ fingerprint combinations for IoT device identification using traffic traces from the CICIoT2023 dataset, with additional validation on the UNSW-IoTraffic dataset. Traffic traces were processed with Zeek to extract the JA4+ fingerprint family, which was evaluated using dictionary-based classification, Random Forest, and Categorical Boosting models. Compact fingerprint representations were compared with decomposed protocol-level features to determine whether feature decomposition improves classification performance or enhances interpretability. Experimental results show that JA4+ fingerprints enable accurate IoT device identification using only passive encrypted traffic metadata. On CICIoT2023, the complete JA4+* configuration achieved a Macro F1-score of 0.8095 with both RF and CatBoost, although this result was obtained on a smaller subset of connections due to fingerprint availability. On the independent UNSW-IoTraffic dataset, CatBoost achieved a Macro F1-score of 0.9995 with both compact and decomposed representations. Overall, decomposed representations did not provide a consistent predictive advantage over compact fingerprints, although they remained valuable for interpretability and feature-level analysis. These findings indicate that compact JA4+ fingerprints can preserve the discriminative information required for IoT device identification without requiring protocol-level decomposition when predictive performance is the primary objective. The results highlight the potential of JA4+ fingerprinting for scalable IoT security monitoring under increasingly encrypted network conditions.
